desc:
For an integer n (it may be negative), return the largest integer r such that r3 ≤ n. In other words, take the real cube root of n and round it down (toward negative infinity).

Examples: 27 gives 3, 26 gives 2, -27 gives -3 and -26 gives -3 (because (-3)3 = -27 ≤ -26 while (-2)3 = -8 > -26).

Do not use a built-in root or power function.
hints: Cubing is increasing for negative numbers too: -3 cubed is smaller than -2 cubed. So "r3 ≤ n" is true for every small r and false for every large r.
You are looking for the last r where that statement is true. First decide a range that must contain it: how large can |r| be when |n| is below 2.2 billion?
Binary search the largest r in [-1291, 1290] with r * r * r ≤ n. Use the upper-middle mid = (lo + hi + 1) // 2 (floor division) so the loop always shrinks, also for negative values.
editorial: The function r → r3 is strictly increasing over all integers, so the predicate "r3 ≤ n" is true up to some threshold and false afterwards. The answer is the last true r.

Since 12903 = 2,146,689,000 < 231 < 12913, the answer lies in [-1291, 1290] (the lower end is reached by n = -231, because (-1291)3 < -231). Search that range with the upper-middle rule. Negative n is where naive code goes wrong: truncating the real cube root toward zero gives -2 for -26, but the floor is -3. Searching the predicate directly avoids any such special case.
